items.title: Million Goods Fort Greene Brooklyn Store Opening | Hypebeast
items.text: Fashion Oct 7, 2026 2.3K Hypes 0 Comments Comments Prefer Hypebeast on Google Save 1 of 9 Million Goods 2 of 9 Million Goods 3 of 9 Million Goods 4 of 9 Million Goods 5 of 9 Million Goods 6 of 9 Million Goods 7 of 9 Million Goods 8 of 9 Million Goods 9 of 9 Million Goods Million Goods has opened its second location, in Fort Greene, Brooklyn The space includes two custom sound systems split across a ground floor bar and listening room, and an upstairs retail floor The store stocks brands like Nicholas Daley, OAMC Peacemaker, Soulland, Rold Skov, LC23, Berner Kühl, Ranra and ssstein Million Goods , a Brooklyn-based retail concept combining independent menswear, hi-fi, natural wine and cultural programming, has opened its second location in Fort Greene, Brooklyn. A roughly 2,100-square-foot space set inside a landmarked building, the new location ports the brand’s DNA from its original Greenpoint location further south in the borough. Founders Drew Kaufmann and Matt Reyer treated the project as an adaptive reuse, keeping the building’s tin ceilings, fireplaces, wood floors and spiral staircase rather than gutting the interior. The store is split into three areas of about 700 square feet each: a bar and listening room on the lower level, a retail floor upstairs and a garden at the rear, visible from the entrance through large windows at the back of the listening floor. The original spiral staircase connecting the two floors is now wrapped in red metalwork, while other details like pecan finished woodwork, honed stone surfaces and limewash paint compliment custom aluminum retail fixtures. Louis Poulsen PH 5 pendants and AJ Eklipta wall lamps illuminate the space while the sound comes Bridge Street Sound designed slim-profile speakers and Million Goods-developed dual-sided speakers, both tuned by Ojas collaborator and sound designer Mo Yasin. The upstairs retail floor carries labels including Nicholas Daley , OAMC Peacemaker , Soulland, Rold Skov, LC23, Berner Kühl, Ranra and ssstein , with Kaufmann and Reyer selecting pieces directly with each brand. Downstairs, the natural wine list centers on France, the Fort Greene location serving a broader by-the-glass selection than Greenpoint. Out back, the garden incorporates the existing trees into the built-in seating with a layout that references Brazilian Brutalism and Japanese garden design. Million Goods Fort Greene is now open Tuesday through Sunday from noon until 10 p.m. on Tuesdays and Sundays, 11 p.m. on Wednesdays, and 12 a.m. on Thursdays, Fridays and Saturdays. The original Greenpoint store continues to operate at 88 Franklin Street. Million Goods Fort Greene 201 DeKalb Avenue Fort Greene, Brooklyn New York City Read Full Article

items.title: Wild Form Design Studio Shapes a Queer Sanctuary in New York | Hospitality Design
items.text: Wild Form Design Studio Shapes a Queer Sanctuary in New York | Hospitality Design News Wild Form Design Studio Shapes a Queer Sanctuary in New York Love Thy Neighbor unfolds as a sculptural, monochromatic space rooted in community and belonging Published: June 2, 2026 By Stephanie Chen Photos by Alexander Tatsuto Zeren + Aichen Mama New York’s West Village has welcomed Love Thy Neighbor , a 40-seat all-day bar and dining concept that gives new meaning to community through hospitality. Brought to life by bartender and restaurateur Shigefumi Kabashima and chef Elias Popa, the intimate venue takes shape as an atmospheric evening cocktail destination, with daytime service forthcoming. At its core, the space is a celebration of the queer community and the joys of chosen family, anchored by a design ethos that embraces fluidity and rejects rigid boundaries. “The idea of ‘no straight lines’ became a guiding principle for us,” says Kabashima. “It reflects not only the design of the space, but also how we think about hospitality: fluid, open, and without boundaries. We want guests to feel a sense of freedom here, both in how they experience the space and how they connect with others.” A hand-shaped environment Collaborating with Jun Qin of Wild Form Design Studio , the founders stripped down traditional church architecture to create a contemporary environment. Vaulted archways and curved, sculpted booths envelop guests in a comforting embrace, grounded by a warm, monochromatic beige palette inspired by sand and earth. “We wanted the entire space to feel as though it was sculpted rather than conventionally assembled, so many of the walls, seating areas, ceilings, and curved transitions were created through hand-shaped cement work,” explains Qin. “The microcement surface finish helps unify the entire environment visually, while also preserving a soft and natural texture throughout the space.” Rather than relying on one dramatic focal point, the architecture relies on cohesive, custom-designed elements. From the niches to the lighting details, the organic curves create a calming, emotional experience. Details to discover at Love Thy Neighbor Throughout the space are details that honor history and community. A single brick from the original Stonewall Inn is embedded within the bar, while a quote from late activist Marsha P. Johnson, which reads “No Pride For Some of Us Without Liberation For All of Us,” is set into the floor at the entrance. “My goal with the space was to embrace our history, paying respect to the literal bricks laid down by our neighbors like the Stonewall Inn, and to create a space that felt warm, embracing, and inclusive,” notes Popa. “Hence, the highlighted brick in the wall at the end of the bar, pulled from Stonewall. A cheeky homage to our shared history.” He continues: “In design, I love when things are clandestine, objects are hidden and only revealed to those who know where to look. This whole bar is an exercise in restraint and subtlety. At the end of the day, we really wanted to create a space that feels transportive, like as soon as you step into the restaurant you feel like you aren’t in New York anymore—even for just a moment.” Posted In: News ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT Related Posts Five on Friday: October 30th, 2026 Chef Thomas Straker Brings His London Restaurant to New York La Fontaine Set To Debut in Century City Early 2027 Marcel Wanders Makes the Case for Taking Risks

items.title: Everything You Need to Know About Skywalker Grill, the Restaurant at the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art — Resy | Right This Way
items.text: Everything You Need to Know About Skywalker Grill, the Restaurant at the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art — Resy | Right This Way Skywalker Grill 4.6 · American · $$ Exposition Park Book Now Published: Oct. 21, 2026 Anyone who grew up with the films of George Lucas knows how rich and immersive a world he can create. Whether in space, amongst ancient ruins and foreign bazaars, or along the streets of 1950’s America, Lucas has shown himself to be a master of visual storytelling. So when it was announced, nearly a decade ago, that the legendary filmmaker would open his Lucas Museum of Narrative Art in Los Angeles, both cinema fans and art lovers around the world rejoiced. Sitting on 11 acres of manicured gardens and housed within a five-story spaceship-like structure designed by renowned architect Ma Yansong, the museum is an act of philanthropy from George Lucas and wife Mellody Hobson. But that gift is not just the 37,000 pieces of art spread across 100,000 square feet of galleries. Lucas has also brought his eye for world-building to Skywalker Grill, the new restaurant perched atop the museum. Like his films, the restaurant leaves no detail overlooked. And visitors to the Lucas having a meal here get a chance to experience one of the filmmaker’s more singular (and most delicious) creations. For chef Diego Cardoso, global vice president of culinary Rhubarb Hospitality, which operates the restaurant, helping Lucas and Hobson create the Skywalker Grill was a dream come true. “Sitting at a table, talking food with George and Mellody, I had to pinch myself,” he says. The Argentina-born chef began his career in the United Kingdom, working under Gordon Ramsay and Angela Harnett at the Connaught Hotel before helping them open London’s Michelin-starred kitchen Murano in 2008. Eventually, he wanted to bring his fine-dining skills to a broader audience. When he joined the team hired to craft Skywalker Grill five years ago, Cardoso’s background aligned perfectly with the vision: a restaurant that could be dressed up or down to serve everyone. Take, for example, the chicken tenders, cured overnight in buttermilk and fried to a golden crisp. They can be served simply with ketchup or ranch, or fancified with crème fraîche and caviar. That flexibility is core to Skywalker’s ethos. “We always say that if we manage to have three generations sitting at the same table, and everybody finds something in the menu that they want to have and eat, then we’re doing a good job,” says Cardoso. Whether you’re dining at the Skywalker Grill for a special occasion, or grabbing a seat in between browsing the museum’s galleries, here’s everything you need to know before you visit: MORE FROM RESY The Rundown Say Hello to Sous Sous, the Buzzy New Restaurant Inside Silver Lake's Hotel Lucile By Kelly Dobkin The Rundown Transport Yourself to the South Pacific at Tiki Residency Savage Seas By Esther Tseng Interviews The Chefs Behind Two Hommés Merge Afrocentric Flavors with L.A. Flair By Elina Shatkin Letter of Recommendation It’s a Celebration Every Night at Manila Inasal By Jean Trinh The dining room offers sweeping views of the city. The dining room offers sweeping views of the city. Fresh produce is at the heart of the menu For the team, keeping dishes light while tapping into the incredible wealth of Southern California’s produce was a key point. Ryan Kluver, formerly of Wally’s and Downtown L.A.’s Patina, who oversees the kitchen day to day, scours the city’s farmers markets for the season’s best produce and seafood. “The lobster salad, with avocado, olive oil, and sweet pepper jus is a really easy dish to eat,” said Cardoso. “Especially sitting there on the terrace in the afternoon and looking out over L.A.—it’s perfect.” George’s memories influenced the menu Hobson made sure the museum offers $2 grilled cheese sandwiches to ensure the museum is accessible to everyone. Lucas also specifically requested a chicken and mushroom crêpe: “He had memories of going to The Magic Pan [a now-defunct chain of crêperies] and loving that,” says Cardoso, noting it might be Lucas’s favorite dish on the menu. And the director also fell hard for the chocolate cake that was a part of Cardoso’s original tasting for the couple. “We almost started the menu working backwards from dessert,” the chef says. The Skywalker Ranch wagyu burger. The Skywalker Ranch wagyu burger. A 360º Skywalker experience One of the most unique aspects of the restaurant is that diners can have a full-circle Skywalker experience. The beef is from the wagyu cattle raised at Lucas’s Marin County compound, Skywalker Ranch. “We’re in a privileged position to work with it,” said Cardoso, who uses the premium meat in the burger, the porterhouse steak, and specials like a tomahawk steak and filet. Meanwhile, honey produced at Skywalker Ranch and a rotating list of vegetables will also be used on the menu. Wines from Skywalker Vineyards will be added soon, giving diners a literal taste of the Skywalker Ranch terroir, one that’s available in no other restaurant. “There are not many projects I’ve done that are so 360°,” says Cardoso. Views from the private dining room. Views from the private dining room. Speaking of wines… Skywalker Grill has a full beverage menu of wine, beer, and cocktails. The wine list leans heavy into Californian and French vintages, which can be ordered both by the glass and the bottle. A Rías Baixas Albariño from Galicia, Spain, stands out of the list of whites, while a bottle from Napa Valley’s Dominus Estate is available from the “Collector’s Cellar” list. A tight beer list offers standards like Modelo and Blue Moon, and a more robust cocktails list ranges from lighter drinks like the Golden Hour (Tanqueray Gin, ancho verde, beets, and lime), to boozier concoctions like the Night Shift (Bullett Rye, Mr. Black coffee liqueur, and Mexican chocolate bitters). As a bonus, the majority of the cocktails can be made non-alcoholic. The interior matches the architecture Not to be outdone by the eye-catching structure, the Skywalker Grill worked with the Rockwell Group (Nobu, Din Tai Fung) to design a sleek yet warm dining room. Dark wood paneling lines the walls and ceiling, as well as large columns intended to evoke the redwood trees of Northern California. Sage green leather banquettes sweep across the room atop the black marble floor. A private dining room tucked in the back of the space houses a dramatic beaded-crystal chandelier, and frosted-glass panes can become opaque in an instant to give a truly private experience. The restaurant also has a large outdoor terrace space where, perched atop the museum, diners get unobstructed views of the Hollywood Hills, Downtown Los Angeles, and Exposition Park below. George Lucas’s beloved chocolate cake. George Lucas’s beloved chocolate cake. A restaurant for all Ultimately, Skywalker Grill is neither a Lucas-themed restaurant nor a museum cafe. It is a space for people to come and enjoy a special meal, whether they’re visiting the Lucas Museum or not. To underscore that point, the restaurant stays open until 8 p.m. most nights (the galleries close at 5), and 10 p.m. on Fridays and Saturdays. In fact, sitting on the terrace as the sun sets is one of Cardoso’s favorite moments: “When the night hits and the lights in the city start to light up—it’s magical.” Oren Peleg is a writer based in Los Angeles. His bylines appear in The New Yorker, Vanity Fair, The Hollywood Reporter, Eater Los Angeles, Architectural Digest, and more. You can follow him here . While you’re at it, follow Resy , too. items.title: Skywalker Grill to Debut as the Signature Dining Destination at the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art - Lucas Museum of Narrative Art
items.text: news Skywalker Grill to Debut as the Signature Dining Destination at the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art Inspired by the hospitality of Skywalker Ranch, the restaurant is now accepting reservations ahead of its September 22 opening August 11, 2026 Copy Link Link Copied Facebook X Threads Skywalker Grill Rendering Credit: Rockwell Group On Tuesday, September 22, 2026, Los Angeles will welcome a new dining destination with the debut of Skywalker Grill , the signature full-service restaurant atop the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art. Designed by Rockwell Group and operated by Rhubarb Events & Hospitality Collection , part of Oak View Group (OVG) , Skywalker Grill draws inspiration from the welcoming spirit of George Lucas' legendary Skywalker Ranch, pairing classic American cuisine with warm hospitality and sweeping views overlooking Los Angeles. Open to both museum visitors and the public, Skywalker Grill welcomes guests for lunch, dinner and weekend brunch, offering a natural extension of a museum visit as well as a place to gather for an evening meal. Remaining open beyond museum hours, the restaurant invites guests to enjoy panoramic views of Los Angeles long after the galleries have closed. “Skywalker Grill is a natural complement to the Lucas Museum experience, offering an inviting space for guests to connect over great food and conversation before or after visiting our galleries,” said Tracey Bates, CEO of the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art. “We are equally excited for it to serve as a destination for Angelenos from across the city to enjoy exceptional hospitality and beautiful surroundings.” Skywalker Grill offers a menu that reflects California-grown ingredients and the enduring appeal of classic American cuisine. Guests can begin with shareable favorites such as Dungeness Crab Cakes and Lobster Corn Dogs, before enjoying signature entrées including Crispy Chicken Milanese, Honey Miso Glazed Salmon and the Skywalker Ranch Wagyu Burger. House-made pastas, fresh seasonal salads and shareable starters round out a menu that is both refined and approachable. "We are incredibly honored to have been part of this remarkable project, and we set out to create a dining experience worthy of it. The menu is inventive yet approachable, designed to welcome everyone. The restaurant's beautiful interiors and thoughtful service were conceived to make it a true Los Angeles destination: a warm, museum-minded hospitality experience that keeps Angelenos and visitors coming back again and again. It is both a tribute to the museum's creative energy and a wonderful reason to dine out," said Katie Harel, Managing Director, Rhubarb Hospitality Collection / Oak View Group Hospitality. Designed by Rockwell Group’s Los Angeles office, Skywalker Grill blends contemporary and Midcentury Modern influences with sculptural architectural forms to create a dining experience that feels both timeless and inviting. Cherry wood wraps the restaurant's walls and ceiling in individually crafted panels, creating warmth and texture throughout the dining room, while softly illuminated white onyx Corian surfaces introduce a subtle sense of light and movement. At the center of the space, a sculptural bar anchors the restaurant, surrounded by intimate seating areas designed to foster conversation and connection. The design extends beyond the main dining room to include an elegant private dining room with switch-glass walls that transition from clear to frosted for added privacy, as well as an outdoor terrace nestled among lush landscaping, offering guests panoramic views of Los Angeles in a relaxed, garden-like setting. "The Lucas Museum celebrates the power of storytelling, and we wanted Skywalker Grill to become part of that narrative," says David Rockwell, Founder and President, Rockwell Group. "Our design echoes the museum’s craftsmanship and innovation while introducing moments of intimacy, warmth, and surprise. From the glowing Corian surfaces to the handcrafted cherry wood detailing, every element was designed to create a sense of wonder that feels tactile and welcoming." Reservations are now available on Resy . For more information, visit www.lucasmuseum.org/skywalker-grill and @skywalkergrill . The Lucas Museum opens its doors on September 22. Tickets are now on sale from opening through February 2027, at lucasmuseum.org . About Skywalker Grill Perched atop the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, Skywalker Grill is the museum's signature full-service restaurant, inspired by the welcoming spirit of George Lucas' Skywalker Ranch. Operated by Rhubarb Events & Hospitality Collection, part of Oak View Group, the restaurant serves refined American cuisine rooted in California's seasonal ingredients alongside a thoughtfully curated beverage program. Open to both museum visitors and the public, Skywalker Grill welcomes guests for lunch, dinner and weekend brunch in a thoughtfully designed space that blends warmth, craftsmanship and panoramic views of Los Angeles. About the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art George Lucas and Mellody Hobson co-founded the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art to honor the universal tradition of telling stories through images. Encompassing everything from prehistoric cave paintings to today’s screen art, the Museum explores and celebrates the power of visual storytelling to inspire individuals, give shape to beliefs and ideals, and forge community. Built in Los Angeles’s Exposition Park, the Museum is housed in a 300,000-square-foot building designed by Ma Yansong of MAD with Stantec to embody the emotional power of narrative art, creating a sense of wonder, possibility, and connection to something larger than ourselves. The building is integrated into a new 11-acre campus including a park designed by Mia Lehrer of Studio-MLA: a green, multilayered gathering place for local communities and an extraordinary programming resource that brings learning and engagement outdoors. About Rockwell Group Rockwell Group is a multidisciplinary architecture and design firm that balances creativity, innovation, and thought leadership with every undertaking. Headquartered in New York City, with offices in Los Angeles and Madrid, the firm was founded in 1984 by David Rockwell, FAIA, and merges performance and architecture to create extraordinary experiences and built environments across the globe. Projects include W Hotels (Hollywood, New York-Union Square, and Naples); Nobu hotels and restaurants worldwide; COTE 550 and Bar Chimera at 550 Madison (New York); The Hand & The Eye (Chicago); Museo Casa Kahlo (Mexico City); Perelman Performing Arts Center (Restaurant and Lobby Interior Architect); The Shed in New York (Diller Scofidio + Renfro, Lead Architect and Rockwell Group, Collaborating Architect); and the 93rd Oscars. Honors include the AIANY President’s Award; a Cooper Hewitt National Design Award; a Tony Award for Best Scenic Design for She Loves Me ; two Emmy Awards for the Oscars; the Presidential Design Award; the James Beard Foundation Who’s Who of Food & Beverage in America; Architectural Digest ’s AD100 Hall of Fame; Interior Design ’s Icon Award; inclusion in Wallpaper * Magazine’s USA 300; and Elle Decor 's A-List. items.title: Skywalker Grill review: Fantasy and fun touch down at the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art | Wallpaper*
items.text: (Image credit: Tom McGovern) Share Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Pinterest Share this article Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter George Lucas has given the world an immense amount of entertainment over the decades, most notably via a dozen Star Wars films. Earlier this month, the filmmaker, along with his wife Mellody Hobson, gave America an otherwordly new cultural destination, The Lucas Museum of Narrative Art – and a restaurant, Skywalker Grill. The restaurant sits at the top of Ma Yansong's otherworldly new building. And like the museum's broader mission, Skywalker Grill is all about the power of visual storytelling, not to mention fresh takes on classic American fare. With views over downtown Los Angeles and references to Lucas' famed Northern California workplace Skywalker Ranch, the destination provides an out-of-this-world place to unwind after a day traipsing through galleries. Here's what to expect. (Image credit: Tom McGovern) Wallpaper* dines at Skywalker Grill The Mood: A galaxy far, far away Designed by Rockwell Group’s Los Angeles office, the restaurant features a generous open floor plan, defined by green-hued leather and velvet banquettes tucked into undulating timber room dividers. The sweeping dining room opens out onto a large dining patio with breathtaking city views. According to firm founder David Rockwell, the design language borrows from midcentury modernism and the idea that architecture can also tell stories. ‘We wanted the restaurant to feel connected to George Lucas’ world through materiality, craftsmanship, imagination and an optimism about the future of design,’ Rockwell says. (Image credit: Tom McGovern) While there are touches of luxe materials throughout (like a bar clad in silver gilt), cherry wood is the primary material, a stylish foil to the building's futuristic space-age envelope; no two panels are alike, thanks to the meticulous work of a local fabricator. ‘The continuous curves and sculpted transitions give the room a sense of movement,’ Rockwell adds. ‘George is naturally drawn to midcentury design and cherry wood is a featured material in his warm and inviting Skywalker Ranch. The space feels almost cinematic in its geometry.’ Wallpaper* Newsletter Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox. (Image credit: Tom McGovern) The food: surprisingly down-to-earth Chef Diego Cardoso, the culinary director for Rhubarb Hospitality Collection and Oak View Group , oversee daily lunch, dinner and weekend brunch menus that lean on California-ingredient-driven American cuisine, along with some childhood comfort food favourites. (Image credit: Tom McGovern) The chicken tenders are a hefty order served with a side of creamy ranch and a generous dollop of caviar. Another sharable hit comes in the form of pigs in a blanket with ballpark-style hotdog bites wrapped around an ‘everything’ croissant, with a spicy mustard dipping sauce. Both are pure comfort and great for bar snacks with a watermelon margarita or coconut martini after a day at the museum. (Image credit: Tom McGovern) For a family meal with the kids, add a signature Skywalker Ranch wagyu burger or mac ’n’ cheese. Lobster salad or honey miso-glazed salmon are lighter options, and surprisingly, so is the chicken mushroom crepe. Large-format plates include pounded-flat crispy chicken Milanese on a bed of fennel and arugula with shaved Parmesan, or the prime New York steak with chimichurri, and herbed French fries, with a wine list that leans heavily on Napa Valley. The rich chocolate layer cake rounds out the meal, and you really won’t need to count calories when you are traversing across the massive museum, library and gardens. While familiar, this is not your typical museum fare, and the modern, futuristic design of the room is a stunning addition to the Lucas legacy. Skywalker Grill is located at the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art , One Lucas Plaza, 3800 S Vermont Ave, Los Angeles, CA 90037, USA TOPICS Carole Dixon Carole Dixon is a prolific lifestyle writer-editor currently based in Los Angeles. As a Wallpaper* contributor since 2004, she covers travel, architecture, art, fashion, food, design, beauty, and culture for the magazine and online, and was formerly the LA City editor for the Wallpaper* City Guides to Los Angeles.

items.text: Commercial Mimi Kakushi Brings Japanese Glamour to Miami Beach 10.29.26 | By Anna Zappia Share on Facebook Share on Pinterest Share on Twitter Share via Email View Slideshow Pirajean Lees brings the glamour of 1920s Osaka and old Hollywood to Mimi Kakushi’s first U.S. location at the Delano Miami hotel. Photography by Robert Reiger. Mimi Kakushi Brings Japanese Glamour to Miami Beach Share on Facebook Share on Pinterest Share on Twitter Share via Email 1/6 Photos Photography by Robert Reiger 2/6 Photos Photography by Robert Reiger 3/6 Photos Photography by Robert Reiger 4/6 Photos Photography by Andrea Di Lorenzo 5/6 Photos Photography by Robert Reiger 6/6 Photos Pirajean Lees brings the glamour of 1920s Osaka and old Hollywood to Mimi Kakushi’s first U.S. location at the Delano Miami hotel. Photography by Robert Reiger. Rooftop lounges are mainstays of the Miami skyline offering open-air escapes above the bustle of the city. For the first U.S. outpost of Japanese restaurant Mimi Kakushi , London-based design firm Pirajean Lees brings together the vibrancy of Miami, the glamour of 1920s Osaka, and the cinematic allure of old Hollywood. Photography by Robert Reiger Clémence Pirajean and James Lees, who also designed the restaurant’s Dubai location, drew inspiration for the Miami interiors from the Japanese silent film actor Sessue Hayakawa. Located on the fourth floor of the Delano Miami hotel, the indoor-outdoor restaurant takes cues from an imagined life for the actor, envisioned as a world traveler whose surroundings reflect different sides of his personality. Photography by Andrea Di Lorenzo That fictional narrative takes shape through a mix of period-inspired details and open-air spaces that connect the restaurant to its coastal setting. The terrace accommodates different dining experiences, from casual gatherings to more intimate meals, and is reserved for hotel guests and Delano Members Club members. Photography by Robert Reiger The open sushi counter places food preparation at the center of the dining experience, giving guests a view of head chef Henry Park’s team at work. A DJ station sets the rhythm throughout the day and evening service, while the bar takes an unconventional approach to presenting its cocktails. Instead of a list of signature cocktails printed on paper, patrons are handed a vintage View-Master to click through reels of drinks featuring botanicals associated with East Asian flavors. Photography by Robert Reiger Lush greenery strategically placed screens divide the terrace into smaller seating areas, providing a sense of enclosure while maintaining ocean views. Counter seating and upholstered banquettes accommodate different ways of dining, whether it’s full-course meals or a selection of shared plates of sashimi and tempura. Sunlight filters through timber bead curtains and stained glass, casting shifting patterns across a palette of warm browns and creams. Fringed throw pillows add texture, while hand-painted landscapes and custom furniture introduce references to traditional craftsmanship. Photography by Robert Reiger Together, the layered materials, shifting daylight, music, and open-air setting create an atmosphere that changes throughout the day. The result is a restaurant that draws on the theatricality of its cinematic inspiration while remaining connected to Miami Beach. Anna Zappia is a New York City–based writer and editor with a passion for textiles, fashion, and design. She can often be found visiting fashion exhibitions or shopping for her next book. items.title: Oyster Estate Greenport: A North Fork Hotel Reimagined
items.text: Travel Oyster Estate Brings a New Design Perspective to Greenport 11.02.26 | By Adrian Madlener Share on Facebook Share on Pinterest Share on Twitter Share via Email View Slideshow At Oyster Estate in Greenport, Islyn Studio pairs the former hotel's mid-century architecture with custom woodwork, natural textures, and details inspired by Long Island's North Fork. Photography by Matt Kisiday. Oyster Estate Brings a New Design Perspective to Greenport Share on Facebook Share on Pinterest Share on Twitter Share via Email 1/11 Photos Photography by Matt Kisiday 2/11 Photos Photography by Matt Kisiday 3/11 Photos Photography by Matt Kisiday 4/11 Photos Photography by Matt Kisiday 5/11 Photos Photography by Matt Kisiday 6/11 Photos Photography by Matt Kisiday 7/11 Photos Photography by Matt Kisiday 8/11 Photos Photography by Matt Kisiday 9/11 Photos Photography by Matt Kisiday 10/11 Photos Photography by Matt Kisiday 11/11 Photos At Oyster Estate in Greenport, Islyn Studio pairs the former hotel's mid-century architecture with custom woodwork, natural textures, and details inspired by Long Island's North Fork. Photography by Matt Kisiday. For years, travelers visiting Long Island’s East End have often found themselves choosing between aging roadside motels or high-priced luxury resorts. Oyster Estate , a new 34-room boutique hotel in the heart of historic Greenport Village, is looking to offer something in between, combining considered design with relaxed, unpretentious comfort. Photography by Matt Kisiday The latest project from Boston-based investment group Blue Flag Capital , Oyster Estate is part of a broader effort to bring new life to the region’s historic hospitality properties. Having already worked on properties including Hotel Corduroy in Montauk and Faraway Sag Harbor , the company has now crossed the Peconic Bay to the North Fork, transforming the longtime Greenporter Hotel. RELATED READING: Faraway Sag Harbor Reimagines a Hamptons Landmark Photography by Matt Kisiday Brooklyn-based Islyn Studio —the practice behind projects including New York’s Brass & Tusk Bar and Mercantile Cafe in Albuquerque—collaborated with Blue Flag Capital on the renovation of the former Greenporter Hotel. Rather than erase the building’s mid-century architectural character, the design team drew inspiration from Greenport’s maritime, agricultural, and winemaking heritage. Instead of relying on overt nautical references, the interiors incorporate these influences through materials, finishes, and carefully considered details. Photography by Matt Kisiday. “We approached the Greenporter with a lot of respect for its history and the role it has played in the community, while recognizing the opportunity to evolve it into something entirely new,” says Brad Guidi, Blue Flag Capital co-founder and chief development officer. “The bones of the property remain, but nearly every aspect of the guest experience was reimagined, drawing inspiration from Greenport’s maritime heritage and creative spirit to create something that feels distinctly rooted in the North Fork.” Photography by Matt Kisiday Custom architectural millwork, wooden built-ins, and layered textiles give the interiors a tactile quality, complemented by locally sourced objects and subtle maritime references. In the lobby, flowers collected in Greenport were dried and pressed into tiles, bringing a tangible piece of the surrounding landscape indoors. Photography by Matt Kisiday Handcrafted details lend the spaces a sense of age and individuality. Both guestrooms and public spaces balance clean architectural lines with warm, natural finishes, creating an environment that feels considered but comfortable. Photography by Matt Kisiday At the physical and social center of the property sits a newly constructed courtyard pool and patio. Designed as a gathering place, the outdoor area gives guests room to lounge and socialize while maintaining the property’s intimate scale. The setting also reflects the North Fork’s quieter coastal character, distinct from the Atlantic-facing beaches of the South Fork. Photography by Matt Kisiday The property’s hospitality offerings are expected to expand with Fortune Favors—an on-site, Asian-inspired bar and dining venue with a hi-fi listening room. Planned features include atmospheric lighting and a custom sound system, extending the hotel’s communal spaces into the evening. Photography by Matt Kisiday With year-round accommodations, Oyster Estate offers visitors a way to experience Greenport beyond the busy summer season. Its combination of preserved architectural character, contemporary interiors, and shared gathering spaces suggests a hospitality model rooted as much in the surrounding community as in the guest experience. Adrian Madlener is a Brussels-born, New York-based writer specializing in collectible and sustainable design. items.text: America ByDESIGN: AmBD | La Padrona La Padrona La Padrona is a perfect balance between design centric goals, Hospitable Thinking, and world class quality food offerings. Split between two unique experiences from the ground floor bar and lounge, up its sculptural grand stair and through the layered second floor signature restaurant, AvroKO’s design team has worked closely with A Street Hospitality - James Beard award-winning Chef Jody Adams, CEO Eric Papachristos, and COO Jon Mendez - to create a space that transports all guests from the Back Bay area of Boston to their custom-designed, post-war, Italian villa. A respectful juxtaposition between traditional Italian details and modern design approaches, the levels are inspired by elements of Gae Aulenti, the glamour of Gold Era Cinema, and the theory and innovation of Dynamism. Guests can acquaint themselves with the lounge and restaurant through many different vantage points and perceive the comprehensive collection of custom lighting and furniture, lush fabrics and upholstery, and high-end architectural materials creates an experience for all the senses. items.title: How This New Orleans Hotel Went From Former Haunted House  to Chic Destination  | Architectural Digest
items.text: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story The Greek Revival mansion that sits at the corner of Prytania Street and Jackson Avenue in New Orleans’ Garden District wouldn’t know “dull” if it came up and rang the doorbell. The 1857 building’s first owner was a cotton merchant who died of yellow fever. Another owner was fatally struck by lightning. Fast-forward to the 21st century, when a Tina Turner impersonator bought the property and turned it into Magnolia Mansion, a B&B with suites with names like Vampire Lovers’ Lair and Moulin Rouge. A former professional boxer and local politics kingmaker took over, but things fell apart around the time of the FBI’s raid on the property. Oh, and the estate is said to be haunted . The Whit's moody mahogany-paneled library Frank Frances Studio The hotel's parlor Frank Frances Studio Named in its B&B era by USA Today as one of the top places in the nation “to sleep with a ghost” the magisterial Harris-Maginnis House earned a spot on the city’s ghost-tour circuit with an ever-mounting pile of lore. According to a spooky tour-operator website , guests at the B&B reported various eerie happenings over the years, such as the sensation of somebody tucking them in at night or a presence watching them while they slept. There were also rumblings of mysterious footsteps and slamming doors. Ghosts or no ghosts, the new team taking over the place found gothic-coded wall murals and dark purple velvet hanging at every turn. Who you gonna call to give an old haunt a new design vernacular? Gretchen Trauth, CEO of the New Orleans investment firm behind the New Orleans hotel, rang up Jensen Logan and Katie Leblanc Killen of Logan Killen, a local design firm known for infusing spaces with a beguiling mix of polish and patina. “The goal was a hotel where nobody can quite tell whether a designer has touched it,” says Logan. Breakfast room with Pierre Frey wallpaper Frank Frances Studio “We wanted it to feel very storied, like it’s been someone’s house for a long time,” adds Killen. “There are these layered histories imbued in the furnishings and the art and accessories.” Named for poet Walt Whitman, who spent three months in New Orleans around the time of the home’s construction, the designers have reimagined the property with a romantic, lived-in, and curio-studded aesthetic that tempts guests to sit down and stay awhile. Architect Seamus McGuire of New Orleans firm Cicada helped navigate historical codes and redraw the map to capture some of the glamour that had drained away in recent years. His blueprint called for converting a trio of bedrooms into lounges. A mahogany-paneled library is now a gallery of antique dog portraits and a repository of volumes from local independent Faulkner House Books. “It’s dark and moody, and where you might want to have a cocktail or a whiskey,” Logan says of the clubby room. Bookworms might also gravitate to the sunroom’s banquette seating, one of the wicker chairs on the wraparound porch , or the breakfast room , a delightfully matchy-matchy enclave covered in Pierre Frey Les Colonnes wallpaper and curtains. The Whit's porch Frank Frances Studio The hardest room to get right, say the designers, was the main lounge. “It’s a giant space that isn’t always in use, and can be tricky to give life to when it’s empty,” says Killen. Intended to serve as a great room by day and an atmospheric cocktail bar come evening, the team layered in elements such as blue paint that reads ethereal by day and warm by night, a custom grid carpet to add a sense of tailoring to the expansive area, and an intimate salon-style wall of works by Louisiana artists, including Robert Moreland and Mallory Page. Another tightrope walk was the second-floor bar. Landmark rules forbid faking history a space never had, so the team went openly Deco instead. “What we don’t want is to put a contemporary bar into a very historic property,” says McGuire. “You can’t give a false sense of history to a space.” One of the hotel's 15 guest rooms Frank Frances Studio It will probably come as little surprise that the bedrooms resist uniformity. In addition to the classically designed units, a quartet of cozy garden rooms has low ceilings and glossy oxblood walls; three cabana rooms feel airy, with bamboo beds and high ceilings. “It’s not meant to feel like everything was changed by the same person at the same time,” Killen says of the narrative that she and Logan have introduced to the New Orleans hotel. As for the supposed ghosts, nobody’s heard boo.
